title: Chimaek for First-Timers: Korea's Fried Chicken and Beer Culture, Explained
html:
If you spend any time in Korea, you'll hear the word chimaek (치맥) sooner or later. It's a mash-up of chi-kin (fried chicken) and maek-ju (beer) — and it's less a menu item than a whole way of hanging out. The good news for a first-time visitor: it's one of the easiest, most walk-in-friendly meals in the country. No booking, no dress code, just a table, some chicken, and a cold drink.

What Is Chimaek, Exactly?

Chimaek pairs Korean-style fried chicken with beer, and it's become a full-blown cultural institution rather than just a snack. It has its own festivals, its own late-night delivery rush, and its own unofficial holiday feeling on Friday nights. The combination took off because Korean fried chicken is double-fried, which makes it lighter and crispier than most Western fried chicken — a texture that pairs especially well with something cold to drink.

Every summer, the Daegu Chimac Festival — Korea's largest food-and-drink festival, drawing roughly a million visitors — turns a city park into days of chicken stalls, concerts, and shared picnic tables. You don't need to travel to Daegu to experience chimaek, though; it's everywhere, from tiny neighborhood pubs to national delivery apps, in every city in Korea.

The Main Types of Fried Chicken to Know

Menus are usually easier than they look — most chicken places boil down to a handful of core styles:

  • Huraideu (후라이드, "fried") — the plain, unsauced original. Crispy, salty, and mild. The safest pick if you're not sure about spice, or if you're ordering for kids.
  • Yangnyeom (양념치킨) — fried chicken tossed in a sweet-and-spicy red sauce (yangnyeom just means "seasoned"). This one has a real kick — not fire-alarm spicy, but noticeably hotter than huraideu, so go in expecting some heat.
  • Ganjang (간장치킨, "soy sauce chicken") — glazed in a savory-sweet soy garlic sauce. No spice at all, just deep, salty-sweet flavor — a good middle ground if yangnyeom sounds like too much.
  • Banban (반반, "half-half") — most places let you order two flavors in one box, split down the middle. Locals order this constantly when a table can't agree, and it's a great way to try yangnyeom without fully committing to it.

Almost every order comes with a free side of chikin-mu (치킨무) — small cubes of sweet pickled radish. It's meant to be eaten alongside the chicken to cut through the oil, not as a separate snack, and it's automatic, not something you order.

Where to Get It: Chicken-Hof Pubs, Chains, and Delivery

A dedicated chicken-and-beer restaurant is often called a chicken-hof (치킨호프, from the German "hof," meaning pub) — expect plastic tables, TVs playing sports, and a menu with photos, which makes ordering easy even without much Korean. Walk-in is completely normal; you'd only need to worry about a wait during a huge live match (Korean baseball or the World Cup, for example) at a very popular spot.

You'll also recognize a handful of big national chains almost everywhere you go — Kyochon, BBQ, bhc, Nene Chicken, and Goobne Chicken are the five you'll spot most often, each with its own signature flavor (Kyochon's soy garlic and BBQ's original recipes are especially popular with first-timers). All of them are sit-down, walk-in friendly, and used to serving takeout and delivery just as often as dine-in.

Here's what locals actually do more than anything: order chimaek for home delivery through an app like Baedal Minjok (Baemin) or Coupang Eats, especially to watch a baseball game or a drama at home. "Let's order chicken" (치킨 시키자) is basically its own casual Friday-night plan in Korea — you don't have to go out to a restaurant to have the full chimaek experience.

What to Drink, and How Locals Pair It

The default pairing is draft beer (생맥주, saeng-maekju), usually served in a large shared pitcher or a tall glass. A popular local twist is somaek (소맥) — a mix of soju and beer stirred together at the table — but it's entirely optional, and nobody will push it on you if you'd rather stick to one drink or skip alcohol altogether. Water and soda are always fine to order instead, and no one will comment on it.

As with restaurants elsewhere in Korea, tipping isn't expected, so there's no need to leave anything extra. When you're ready to go, either flag down a server or look for a buzzer on the table, and pay at the counter near the entrance — most chicken-hofs take foreign credit cards, but it's smart to carry a little cash for smaller, older-school spots.

Whichever flavor you start with, chimaek is meant to be shared slowly over a couple of hours, not rushed — so pull up a plastic chair, order a whole chicken for the table, and see why it's become such a fixture of a night out in Korea.

Style Flavor Spice Level Best For
Huraideu (Original) Crispy, plain, salty None Kids, spice-sensitive travelers, first-timers
Yangnyeom Sweet-and-spicy red sauce Mild–Medium The classic chimaek experience, adventurous eaters
Ganjang (Soy Garlic) Savory-sweet, garlicky None Flavor without any heat
Banban (Half & Half) Two flavors in one order Depends on picks Groups, first-timers who can't decide

💬 Not sure which flavor to start with, or want a chicken-hof recommendation near where you're staying? Drop a comment — happy to help you plan your first chimaek night!
meta_description: A beginner's guide to chimaek, Korea's beloved fried chicken and beer combo: the main flavors to know, where to eat walk-in, and how locals actually drink it.
